_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season9-bible-v1.0.0.md row a9e01 and writer brief a9e01-v1.0.0.md. a8e07's next field was honoured: the AI system design interview framework in plain words: requirements, data, model choice, evals, safety and cost. Keeps apart from a5e01 (the test set is one step of six) and a8e01 (here nobody asked the right questions; the facts did not change). Halloween is only the week: costumes are stock with sizes, nothing supernatural. Timeline: the website assistant went live on Monday 12 October 2026 with a large model, the 40 help pages in its instructions and 50 test questions written from those pages (47 of 50); no stock list and no order diary connected. Until Monday 26 October most sizes were in stock, so product-page answers were usually true by luck; ready-by answers were caught at the counter, where arches and banners are ordered after the diary is checked. The children's skeleton costume in age 7 to 8 sold out on Tuesday 27 October. Thursday 29 October: the father's chat at 18:52, shown at the counter at 19:20; close at 21:00; she checks tonight's 40 chats (18:00 to 21:00): 31 stock and size (3 right), 3 ready-by (0), 6 general (6), 9 of 40; she sorts 200 chats picked across 12 to 28 October: 124 stock and size, 30 ready-by, 46 general; her test covered the general kind, 46 of 200. Interview 10:00 Friday 30 October; Halloween Saturday 31 October. Given in the sim: a real-mix test of 50 (31 stock with 5 sizes in stock and 1 costume described, not named; 8 ready-by, all for a full Saturday; 11 general, all answered right); as built 16 of 50, the fix 49 of 50; tonight with both lookups and the stock-only rule 39 of 40, 0 wrong, 1 sent to the shop. Sources read 16 October 2026; the ISO pages are third-party summaries.
title: The Framework
setting: a party shop in Halloween week

post.author: u/costume_rail_xiomara
post.title: I run the evening shift at a party shop and built its website assistant for my portfolio. Its test says 47 of 50. Of tonight's 40 chats, 9 were right.

blocks.text: I'm the evening shift leader at an independent party shop: costumes, balloons, decorations. It's Halloween week, so we're open until 21:00. By day I study to become an AI engineer, someone who builds products on top of existing AI programs. My first AI system design interview is at 10:00 on Friday 30 October: an hour of designing a system out loud.

My portfolio project is the shop's website assistant, live since Monday 12 October. A customer types a question into a chat box on our website, and it replies. Under it sits a language model, a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text. I chose a large one.

Its instructions, the standing text it reads before every chat, hold all 40 of our help pages: hours, returns, helium rules, order times. To check it, I wrote 50 test questions from those pages, each with its right answer. It got 47 right.

I never connected our stock list. The till keeps it: each sale takes one off that costume and size, and each delivery we count in adds to it. I never asked the owner what customers actually message about, either.

Tonight is Thursday 29 October. The assistant's panel, its page of numbers, still says: test score 47 of 50. At 19:20 a father at the counter showed me a chat on his phone. Each line shows the time, who wrote, and what they wrote.

18:52  customer   do you have the skeleton costume in age 7 to 8?
18:52  assistant  Yes, the skeleton costume comes in age 7 to 8.
Its product page lists ages 3 to 4, 5 to 6, 7 to 8 and 9 to 10. Age 7 to 8 sold out on Tuesday.
Every size it is made in. Not one it has.

We close at 21:00. Afterwards I checked tonight's 40 chats, 18:00 to 21:00, against the stock list, the till and our order diary, the book where each balloon arch and printed banner is written against the day it's due. 9 were right.

Then I took 200 chats, picked across 12 to 28 October, and sorted them by kind, meaning what each one asks about. I read each, put it on one of three piles, and counted. 124 were stock and size. 30 asked if something could be ready by a day. 46 were general: hours, returns, helium. All 50 test questions were the general kind: they tested 46 of the 200.

Tonight's 40 split the same way. 31 stock and size: 3 right, the three sizes still on the shelf. 3 ready-by, all for Saturday: none right. Saturday's diary page is full, and the assistant answered from a help page: order by 12:00 the day before. 6 general: all right. 3 + 0 + 6 = 9.

Until Monday most sizes were in stock, so its answers were usually true by luck. This week most children's sizes of the popular costumes sold out. Ready-by answers never mattered: arches and banners are only ordered at the counter, after we check the diary.

blocks.text: Halloween is Saturday. My interview is at 10:00. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your shop is haunted, not even the skeleton. A model only sees the text sent with each chat. Two questions. When it said 'comes in age 7 to 8', did it have a stock lookup? That would be a small tool (a2e05): the assistant's program runs it when the model asks, and it reads the till's count for one costume and size. Or did it only have the product page? And of your 50 test questions, how many asked about stock or a date?

replies.author: u/costume_rail_xiomara
replies.text: Only the product page, and no tool at all. None of the 50. I wrote them from the help pages, and the help pages don't know what's on the shelf.

comments.author: u/pass_mark_tjitske
comments.text: 47 of 50 is a pass in any exam. Sold-out sizes are a stock problem, not an assistant problem: the shop ran out, and the help pages didn't change. If you want to walk into that interview sure of your project, write 50 more test questions from the help pages and score it again. A bigger test is a stronger claim.

replies.author: u/costume_rail_xiomara
replies.text: The father's question isn't on any help page.

comments.author: u/one_more_line_yaretzi
comments.text: Simplest fix: add one line to its instructions, 'never guess about stock'. Free, and live tonight.

replies.author: u/costume_rail_xiomara
replies.text: I tried it on the father's question at 22:30. Same answer. The product page says the costume comes in age 7 to 8, so to the model that isn't a guess.

reply.prompt: Halloween is on Saturday, and her interview is at 10:00 on Friday. What should she change about the assistant, and how she built it? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Swap in a bigger model that knows more about costumes and party goods.
options.part2: At 01:00 I switched to the biggest model I could pay for. Its help-page test: 47 of 50 again. Then I replayed tonight's 40 chats on it: 9 right, again. 3 of 31 stock and size, 0 of 3 ready-by, 6 of 6 general. To the father's question it said, in nicer words, that the skeleton costume comes in age 7 to 8. It had read more about costumes and been shown nothing about our shelves, because nothing had changed in what it could see. It also costs more for every chat. At 10:00 the interviewer asked where I'd start designing an assistant for a shop's website. I started with the model, and she stopped me there.
options.senior: A bigger model writes better from what it is given, but the stock list is not in what it is given. Every miss tonight came from missing data, not weak writing, so the count stays at 9 of 40 and only the price per chat goes up. Choosing the model before asking what customers ask and what data exists is the step the AI system design round is built to catch.

options.text: Write 50 more test questions from the help pages and score it again.
options.verdict: A bigger test of the same 46 of 200
options.part2: By 03:00 I had 50 more questions from the help pages, written the same way, and the panel read 94 of 100. It looked stronger. But all 100 came from the same 40 pages, so they still tested only the general kind: 46 of the 200 real chats. Replaying tonight's 40 gave 9 again. On Friday the three ready-by customers came to the counter for their Saturday arches, and the diary was full. At the interview I quoted 94 of 100. The interviewer asked what customers message about. I didn't know.
options.senior: More questions from the same source measure the same thing more precisely. A test written from the help pages can only score what the help pages answer, so it covered 46 of 200 real chats at 50 questions and still at 100. A test earns its number by mirroring what real users ask, sorted and scored by kind.

options.text: Sort 200 real messages by kind, add a stock lookup, then choose.
options.part2: At 01:30 I added one rule in code first: the assistant may say a size is in stock only when a stock lookup says so. Until a lookup existed, every stock question got 'please ask in the shop'. At 10:00 the interviewer asked me to design an assistant for a shop's website: where do I start? I started with who messages us and about what, and showed her my piles: 124, 30, 46. After the interview the owner gave the assistant read-only access to the till's stock list and to the order diary: two lookups. With the lookups doing the knowing, I chose a small model. I picked a new test of 50 from the real chats in the same mix, 31 stock and size, 8 ready-by and 11 general, and scored each kind on its own: 49 of 50, the same as the large model. It went live at 18:00 on Friday. Replaying Thursday's 40: 39 right, 0 wrong. The one left over described a costume in our window instead of naming it; the lookup found nothing, so the rule sent it to the shop. On the card by the till I wrote: what do customers actually ask?
options.senior: Start from requirements: read real messages and count them by kind, because that is the job. Then ask what data each kind needs and how fresh it is: the stock list changes with every sale, so it has to be looked up, not pasted in. Only then choose the model, often a small one once lookups do the knowing. Build the test from the real mix and score each kind, add the rule that stock is stated only from the lookup, and count the price per chat. That order is what the AI system design round tests.

options.text: Turn off stock and order answers; tell customers to ask in the shop.
options.part2: From 01:00, any stock, size or ready-by question got one answer: 'please ask in the shop'. Replaying tonight's 40: 6 right, 0 wrong, 34 sent to the counter. Nothing false went out again. But across the 200 real chats it now answered 46 and turned away 154, the very questions customers came to it with, in the busiest week of the year. On Friday the counter queue reached the door, and the owner asked what the assistant was for. At the interview I said I had made it safe. The interviewer asked what it was safe at doing.
options.senior: Refusing what you can't check is honest, and it is the right fallback while a lookup is being built. As the design, it drops 154 of every 200 messages, the work customers wanted. The better answer keeps the rule and gives the assistant the data to answer, so 'please ask in the shop' is left for the few it cannot check.

sim.title: Replay the party shop's chats, question by question
sim.lede: You're the evening shift leader at 17:59 on Thursday 29 October, before the evening's first chat. No real model runs here: each answer follows a stated rule over given counts. Given: 200 chats picked across 12 to 28 October, 124 stock and size, 30 ready-by, 46 general. Tonight's 40, 18:00 to 21:00: 31 stock and size (3 ask for sizes still in stock; 1 of the sold-out 28 describes a costume in the window instead of naming it), 3 ready-by, all for Saturday, whose diary page is full, and 6 general. The help-page test: 47 of 50; 50 more written the same way also score 47, so 94 of 100; its 3 misses are about how long helium balloons float, where two help pages disagree. A real-mix test: 50 picked from the 200 in about the same mix, 31 stock and size (5 in stock, 1 described), 8 ready-by (all for Saturday) and 11 general (all answered right). The rules: without a stock lookup, a stock answer comes from the product page and is right only if the size is in stock; with it, every named costume is right, and the described one is guessed from the product page (wrong) unless the stock-only rule, a check in code that blocks any stock claim the lookup didn't make, sends it to the shop. Without the order diary, every ready-by gets a wrong yes. General answers are right whatever the model's size. Sending stock and order answers to the shop sends all of them.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as built, the panel says 47 of 50. Play tonight: 9 of 40, 3 + 0 + 6. Switch to the larger model: still 9. Score 100 help-page questions: 94 of 100, still 46 of 200. Switch to the real-mix test: 16 of 50. Turn on the stock lookup and the order diary: 39 of 40, but 1 wrong; add the stock-only rule: 0 wrong, 1 sent to the shop, and 49 of 50. Then send stock and order answers to the shop: 154 of 200 turned away. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the party shop was haunted. The assistant was built model first: a large model, 40 help pages and a test written from those pages, so 47 of 50 measured only the general kind, 46 of 200 real chats. It could not see the stock list or the order diary, so when sizes sold out in Halloween week, tonight's answers came to 3 + 0 + 6 = 9 of 40. Nobody had asked what customers actually ask.

steps.title: Six questions, in order.
steps.text: An AI system design answer usually walks six questions, each answered before the next. First, requirements: who asks, about what, how many, how fast, and what must never happen. Second, data: what exists, where it lives and how fresh it is. Third, model choice: the smallest model that does the job with that data. Fourth, evals: a test built from real requests and scored per kind. Fifth, safety: rules for what the system must never say. Sixth, cost: the price per request times how many come. What can go wrong: starting at question three, the model, which is what happened here, and every later answer then rests on a guess about the first two.

steps.title: Requirements and data: the two questions she skipped.
steps.text: Requirements start with real messages. She read 200 chats, put each on a pile by kind and counted: 124 stock and size, 30 ready-by, 46 general. Then data: stock and size answers need the stock list, and the till changes it with every sale, so it must be read at the moment of the question, through a stock lookup, a tool (a2e05). Ready-by answers need the order diary in the same way. A help page pasted into instructions is a copy that never changes. What can go wrong: the product page lists every size a costume is made in, and a model reading it will answer 'comes in age 7 to 8' long after the last one sold.

steps.title: Model choice comes after the data.
steps.text: With the lookups doing the knowing, the model's job is to read a message, ask the right lookup and say the answer plainly. A small model was enough: on the real-mix test it scored 49 of 50, the same as the large one. A bigger model would have changed nothing tonight; in the replay it still gets 9 of 40, because no model can read a stock list it is never shown. What can go wrong: a smaller model can miss things a larger one gets, so the choice is checked on the test, not assumed.

steps.title: Evals from real messages, scored per kind.
steps.text: Her 50 questions came from the help pages, so they only measured what the help pages answer: the general kind, 46 of 200. Fifty more of the same made 94 of 100 and still covered 46 of 200. A golden set (a5e01) is only as good as where its questions come from. The real-mix test takes 50 from the real chats in about the same mix, 31 stock and size, 8 ready-by, 11 general, and scores each kind on its own, so a weak kind can't hide in the total. As built it scores 16 of 50; with both lookups and the rule, 49 of 50. What can go wrong: the mix changes with the season, so re-sort a fresh sample before every busy week.

steps.title: Safety, then cost.
steps.text: The safety rule is a check in code, not a line in the instructions: the assistant may say a size is in stock only when the lookup says so. A line saying 'never guess' changed nothing, because to the model the product page was not a guess. With the rule, tonight's replay is 39 of 40 right, 0 wrong and 1 sent to the shop: a costume described, not named. Cost comes last: about 40 chats a night this week, at a small model's price per chat. What can go wrong: turning off every stock and order answer is safe too, but it drops 154 of every 200 messages.

diagram.aria: The six questions in order, with the party shop's answers. Top row: 1, requirements, 200 chats sorted by kind into 124, 30 and 46; 2, data, the stock list and the order diary, fresh to the last sale; 3, model choice, a small model with two lookups, where the model's size changes no count. Bottom row: 4, evals, 50 questions from the real mix, 49 of 50, scored per kind; 5, safety, stock stated only from the lookup, 0 wrong and 1 sent to the shop; 6, cost, about 40 chats a night at a small model's price.

notes.text: Answer each question before the next

explain.caption: Read left to right, top row then bottom: requirements from 200 real chats sorted by kind; the data each kind needs, looked up fresh; then the model, small once the lookups do the knowing; a test from the real mix, scored per kind; the rule that stock is stated only from the lookup; and the price of about 40 chats a night.

fix.title: The fix: start again from requirements, and choose the model last
fix.text: Sort a sample of real messages by kind: here 124 stock and size, 30 ready-by and 46 general of 200. Give each kind the data it needs, read fresh: a stock lookup on the stock list the till keeps, and a lookup on the order diary. Then choose the model; a small one was enough. Build the test from the real mix, 31, 8 and 11 of 50, and score each kind on its own. Add a rule in code that stock is stated only from the lookup, so anything the lookup can't find goes to the shop. Count the price per chat. Tonight's replay goes from 9 of 40 to 39 of 40, with 0 wrong.

limits: The sort is only as good as its sample. 200 chats from 12 to 28 October may under-count questions that only come up in the last days before Halloween or in the January sale, so re-sort a fresh sample before each busy season.
A lookup is only as fresh as what it reads. A costume sold at the counter a second after the lookup will still be promised, and the stock list is wrong whenever a delivery isn't counted in.
The sim treats every model size alike. In real use a smaller model can miss phrasings a larger one handles, so the size is chosen by scoring each candidate on the real-mix test.

explain.seniorTake: Most AI systems that disappoint were built model first: someone picked a model, gave it the documents at hand, wrote a test from the same documents and got a high score. The score was true and answered the wrong question. Start from requirements: read real requests and count them by kind, because the mix is the job. Then ask what data each kind needs and how fresh it must be; anything that changes by the hour, like stock or bookings, has to be looked up at the moment of the question, not pasted into instructions. Only then choose the model, usually the smallest that does the job once the lookups do the knowing. Test on the real mix and score each kind on its own. Put the rules about what must never be said in code that checks the lookup, not in a sentence the model may ignore. Count the price last, at the real volume. In an interview, that order is the answer: the round is testing whether you ask before you build.

realWorld.title: Huyen, 2022: start with why
realWorld.text: Chip Huyen's summary of chapter 2 of Designing Machine Learning Systems, Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design, says: Every project must start with why this project needs to happen, and ML projects are no exception. The shop's why was customers' real questions, which nobody counted.

realWorld.title: Huyen, 2022: business objectives become model objectives
realWorld.text: The same summary says business objectives need translating: which need to be translated into ML objectives to guide the development of ML models. It then names four general requirements for the system: reliability, scalability, maintainability, and adaptability. In the shop, the business objective is customers told the truth about stock; 47 of 50 on help pages was never translated from it.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: evals that mirror real use
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide, Define success criteria and build evaluations, lists as an eval design principle: Be task-specific: Design evals that mirror your real-world task distribution. Don't forget to factor in edge cases! The real-mix test does this; the costume described instead of named is an edge case.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: success criteria you can measure
realWorld.text: The same guide asks for criteria that are specific and measurable, and says: Measurable: Use quantitative metrics or well-defined qualitative scales. Here that is a count per kind with its denominator, such as 30 of 31 stock and size questions right, not one total.

realWorld.title: ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.2: requirements before work
realWorld.text: A certification body's guide summarises clause 8.2 as: This section ensures that customer requirements are clearly understood and agreed before work begins. On determining requirements it adds: Nothing should be assumed. That is the guide's summary, not the standard's own text.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: requirements, then verification
realWorld.text: A third-party guide to Annex A describes control A.6.2.2 as specifying and documenting requirements for new or significantly enhanced AI systems, and A.6.2.4 as asking organisations to establish robust verification and validation measures for AI systems. The guide's wording, not the standard's; check your own copy.

asked: Design an assistant for a shop's website: where do you start?
Walk me through how you structure an AI system design answer.
interview.answer: I'd start with requirements, before any model. Who writes to the shop, about what, how many a day, how fast they need an answer, and what must never happen, such as promising a size that's sold out. I'd ask for a sample of real messages, a couple of hundred, and sort them by kind; at a party shop that might be stock and size, ready-by dates and general questions, and the counts tell me what the system is for. Then data: for each kind, what holds the answer, where it lives and how fresh it is. Stock changes with every sale, so it needs a lookup tool on the till's stock list, not a copy in the instructions; dates need the order diary. Then the model: with lookups doing the knowing, I'd try the smallest model that passes. Then evals: a test drawn from the real mix, scored per kind, so a weak kind can't hide. Then safety: a check in code that the assistant states stock only when the lookup says so, and sends anything it can't check to a person. Last, cost: the price per chat times the real volume, about 40 a night in the busiest week. If the shop works to ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 42001, the sorted requirements and the per-kind test are also the records those standards look for. The AI system design round is testing that order.

terms.def: A shop that sells costumes, balloons and decorations. In Halloween week this one stays open until 21:00.
The person in charge of the shop floor and the till from late afternoon until closing. The storyteller is one.
Someone who builds products on top of existing AI models: assistants, lookups, tests. The storyteller is studying to become one.
A job interview round of about an hour in which a candidate designs an AI system out loud, such as an assistant for a shop's website, and explains each choice.
Something a job seeker builds to show what they can do. Hers is the shop's website assistant.
The program that answers customers in a chat box on the shop's website, live since Monday 12 October. A language model writes its replies.
A program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown very large (a1e01). Also called a model.
Language models differ in size. Larger ones usually write better and cost more for every chat; smaller ones are cheaper and often enough when lookups supply the facts.
The standing text a model reads before every chat. Hers held all 40 help pages, pasted in once: a copy that never changes.
The shop website's 40 pages on hours, returns, helium rules and order times. They say nothing about what is on the shelf today.
Questions with their right answers, used to score a system. Hers were 50, written from the help pages: 47 of 50 right.
The assistant's page of numbers. On Thursday 29 October it still read: test score 47 of 50.
The shop's count of every costume in every size. The till takes one off with each sale, and each delivery counted in adds to it.
The shop's checkout, where each sale is rung up. It keeps the stock list up to date.
A costume's page on the website, listing every size it is made in, such as ages 3 to 4, 5 to 6, 7 to 8 and 9 to 10, whether or not any are left.
The book where each balloon arch and printed banner is written against the day it is due. Saturday 31 October's page is full.
What a message asks about. She sorted 200 chats into three kinds: stock and size (124), ready-by (30) and general (46).
A customer asking if something can be ready by a day, such as a balloon arch for Saturday. The answer is in the order diary.
A tool the model can ask your code to run: it reads the till's stock list for one costume and size and returns the count at that moment.
A small job your app offers a model, like a button the model can ask you to press. The model only asks; your code runs it (a2e05).
Able to look things up but not change them. The assistant's lookups can read the stock list and the diary, never edit them (a2e05).
50 questions picked from the 200 real chats in about the same mix, 31 stock and size, 8 ready-by and 11 general, each kind scored on its own.
A check in code: the assistant may say a size is in stock only when the stock lookup says so. Anything the lookup can't find goes to the shop.
What a system must do, for whom and how well: who asks, about what, how many, how fast, and what must never happen. The first of the six questions.
Six questions answered in order: requirements, data, model choice, evals, safety, cost. Each answer shapes the next.
A test of an AI system's quality: questions with known good answers and a way to score the replies (a1e01, a5e01).
A fixed list of real inputs with the right answers agreed in advance, kept to score every version of a system (a5e01).
An unusual input at the limits of what a system expects, like a costume described from the window instead of named.
What the business needs from a system, in its own terms, such as customers told the truth about stock. Huyen says model objectives should be translated from it.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 8.2 covers determining and reviewing requirements for products and services before work begins.
The international standard for an AI management system. Annex A includes controls on AI system requirements (A.6.2.2) and verification and validation (A.6.2.4).
The course's final build milestone, Walk me through Nightwatch. It unlocks after s9e05, a9e01 and a9e04, and its walkthrough follows this case's six questions.

atWork: Look for an AI feature built model first. It is a common pattern: a team picks a model, gives it the documents at hand, writes test questions from those same documents and ships on a high score. The first sign of trouble is usually a question the documents never answered, about something that changes by the hour: stock, bookings, prices, delivery dates. Ask five things. Has anyone sorted a sample of real requests by kind, and what are the counts? For each kind, where does the answer live and how fresh is it? Was the model chosen before or after that? Is the test drawn from the real mix and scored per kind? Is there a check in code for what must never be said? Build Night: X7, Walk me through Nightwatch, unlocks after s9e05, a9e01 and a9e04, and this case's six questions are the order of its walkthrough: requirements, data, model, evals, safety, cost. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation works to ISO 9001:2015, clause 8.2 (as summarised by certification bodies) expects requirements to be determined and reviewed before work begins; if it is certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 or working toward it, Annex A controls A.6.2.2 (requirements and specification) and A.6.2.4 (verification and validation), as third-party guides summarise them, point the same way. Keeping the sorted sample, the per-kind test and the rule as records from the first build costs far less than reconstructing them for an auditor.

recall.prompt: A gym asks you to build a website assistant for its members. You have its 60 FAQ pages and a week. Your teammate has already picked the largest model and written 40 checks from the FAQ pages, and it scores 38 of 40. What do you do first, and why?

keyIdeas.idea: Start from requirements: read a sample of real member messages and sort them by kind before anything else
For each kind, find the data that holds the answer and how fresh it is, read through a lookup
Build the test from the real mix and score each kind, then choose the model

recall.model: Before the model, the requirements: I'd read a sample of real messages from members, a couple of hundred, and sort them by kind, because 38 of 40 only says the assistant answers what the FAQ pages answer. If many ask about class times or bookings, the answer lives in the booking system and changes by the hour, so I'd ask how fresh each kind's data is and read it through a lookup tool, not paste it in. Then I'd build the test from the real mix, score each kind on its own, and only then choose the model, the smallest that passes.

recall.prompt: The shop's 200 real chats sorted into 124 stock and size, 30 ready-by and 46 general. Her 50 checks were all written from the help pages and were all the general kind. How much of the real traffic did they test?
recall.why: Only the general kind, 46 of the 200 real chats, about 23%. 47 of 50 is the score on that kind alone; 154 of 200 is what the help-page test never touched, and the 124 stock and size chats were most of it.

recall.prompt: An interviewer asks: walk me through how you structure an AI system design answer, and why the order matters.

keyIdeas.idea: Requirements first: who asks, about what, how many, and what must never happen
Then data: what exists, where it lives and how fresh it is; the model is chosen after that
Then evals from real requests per kind, safety rules in code, and the price at real volume

recall.model: I start with requirements: who asks, about what, how many, how fast, and what must never happen, ideally from a sorted sample of real requests. Then data: what exists, where it lives and how fresh it is, which decides whether it can be pasted in or must be looked up. Then the model, the smallest that does the job with that data. Then evals built from real requests and scored per kind; then safety, rules checked in code; then the price per request at the real volume. The order matters because each answer shapes the next: start with the model and every later step rests on a guess.

recall.prompt: Replaying Thursday's 40 chats with the stock lookup and the order diary connected, but no stock-only rule, gives 39 right and 1 wrong. What does adding the rule change?
options: The 1 wrong is sent to the shop instead; still 39 right
It turns away 154 of every 200 messages
Nothing, because the lookup already checks stock
recall.why: The one miss describes a costume in the window instead of naming it, so the lookup finds nothing and the model guesses from the product page. The rule blocks any stock claim the lookup didn't make, so that chat goes to the shop: 39 right, 0 wrong, 1 sent on.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. The assistant has run on the two lookups and a small model since Friday 30 October, and the real-mix test still reads 49 of 50. In November the owner started delivering balloon arches to parties, booked by phone. Last week he asked me to put delivery bookings into the assistant before New Year's Eve. He has already chosen a model a friend recommends for bookings, and he wrote 20 test questions from the new delivery price list. It scores 19 of 20.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Where should she start, and in what order?

keyIdeas.idea: Start again from requirements: collect real delivery requests and sort them by kind before keeping his model
Find the data each kind needs and how fresh it is, such as the van's free slots, through a read-only lookup
Test on the real mix per kind and add a rule that a slot is only promised when the lookup says it is free

coldCase.model: Not with the model, and not with 19 of 20 from the price list: that test only scores what the price list answers. Start from requirements: pull the real requests from his phone notes since November and sort them by kind; most are probably 'can you deliver on this date?'. Then data: those need the delivery diary's free slots, which change with every booking, so give the assistant a read-only lookup on them. Only then choose the model, the smallest that passes. Build the test from the real mix and score each kind, and add a rule in code to never confirm a slot unless the lookup shows it free. Then count the price per chat.
